Q: Trying to create a log file in sharepoint A:

You need to Set the Workbook object to the book you are opening.

Set wb = Workbooks.Open()

You don't need a loop to transfer this data from one sheet to another. You can transfer all of the data with a single operation which would be the best practice method.

Here's 3 examples below:



Option Explicit
Private Sub Workbook_BeforeClose(Cancel As Boolean)

'CURRENT BOOK:Determine range with logs to copy starting at A2.
  Dim ws As Worksheet, lr As Long, lc As Long, copy_logs As Range
        Set ws = ThisWorkbook.Sheets("!!!!")        '<--- Update sheet name
            lr = ws.Range("A" & ws.Rows.Count).End(xlUp).Row
            lc = ws.Cells(1, ws.Columns.Count).End(xlToLeft).Column
                Set copy_logs = ws.Range(ws.Cells(1, 2), ws.Cells(lr, lc))
                
            
            
'LOG BOOK: Find paste destination to append log file instead of overwriting
        Dim fp As String, logWB As Workbook, log As Worksheet
        Dim pr As Long, paste_logs As Range   'pr = Paste Row (first empty row)
            fp = ("https:/[companySP]/logs.xlsx")       'File path
            Set logWB = Workbooks.Open(fp)
            Set log = logWB.Sheets("log list")
    
        
                pr = log.Range("A" & log.Rows.Count).End(xlUp).Offset(1).Row
                
                '------- 3 METHODS TO WRITE LOGS WITHOUT LOOPS ---------
                
                '1) Range transfer is most effecient if you you only need values
                Set write_logs = log.Range("A" & size).Resize(lr - 1, lc - 1)
                write_logs.Value = new_logs.Value
                
                '2) Standard copy/paste which retains cell formatting, formulas,etc
                copy_logs.copy log.Range("A" & pr)
                
                '3) Copy and choose attributes to paste
                copy_logs.copy
                log.Range("A" & pr).PasteSpecial (xlPasteValues)
        
        'Close & save log book
        'Other closing processes
    
End Sub

Note: if there's ever a chance that your main workbook creates no logs over the course of the session, I would recommend modifying the code accordingly. (If 0 new_logs then End' for example)

Q: fork in multi-threaded program A:

Forking inside a multithreaded program is risky because fork() only copies the calling thread into the child, not the other threads. The child receives a snapshot of memory, including mutex states, which may be inconsistent since other threads disappear. This can cause deadlocks or undefined behavior. For this reason, the child should usually call exec() immediately after fork()

Q: bash script error converting zip file to tar.gz (or tar.bz2) A:

  • What unzip -p does: The -p flag stands for "extract to pipe." It sends the actual contents (the text, binary data, etc.) of the files inside the ZIP directly to standard output.

  • What tar --files-from=- expects: This flag tells tar to read a list of filenames from standard input.

The result: You are feeding the internal data of your files into tar and telling it that this data is a list of filenames to look for on your hard drive. Since your hard drive doesn't have files named after the content of your ZIP files, tar returns "File not found" errors.

To convert a ZIP to a TAR without extracting to disk, you generally cannot use standard unzip and tar together in a simple pipe because tar needs to know file boundaries and names, which unzip -p strips away.

The most common "simple" bash solution is to extract to a temporary directory first:

Bash

mkdir temp_extract
unzip "$2.zip" -d temp_extract
tar -zcvf "$2.tar.gz" -C temp_extract .
rm -rf temp_extract

Alternatively, if you have bsdtar installed (common on macOS and many Linux distros), it can handle multiple formats natively:

Bash

bsdtar -xf "$2.zip" -cf "$2.tar.gz"

Q: Detecting a face with OpenCV A:

You have to use the detector you created.

Just because the running mode is live stream doesn't mean the detector object knows which live stream. You've directed data out of it with the callback, but haven't directed data into it. Consider that you need to create the cap object because it refers to a specific live stream - you can even switch the stream or feed a mix of multiple streams into your detector if you wanted.

Looks like you used code from one section of Google's guide? The subsequent sections tell you how to feed frames into the detector:

mp_image = mp.Image(image_format=mp.ImageFormat.SRGB, data=frame)
detector.detect_async(mp_image, timestamp_ms)

Notice that the detector works asynchronously here. This is standard practice as detection can be slow and block the program (or a website) from doing something else in the meanwhile, e.g. responding to some user inputs. It's also why you're giving it a callback - once you're done processing a frame, you do whatever is needed with the result. You can put imshow and anything related like drawing a detected bounding box into the callback as well.

The variable timestamp_ms is necessary because of this async approach to give an ordering to outputs (which are fed into the callback function). Just set it to 0 before your loop and update it in the loop by however many milliseconds you wait.
